reference.source: Smith's Recognizable Patterns of Human Malformation / Nelson Textbook of Pediatrics
clinicalPearls: Presents with disproportionate short-limbed short stature that is usually not apparent at birth but emerges as growth slows in the second year of life
Caused by autosomal dominant variants in COMP encoding cartilage oligomeric matrix protein, which accumulates abnormally within chondrocytes
The head and face are normal, distinguishing it clinically from achondroplasia, but there is marked ligamentous laxity and early progressive joint pain
Radiographs show generalised epiphyseal and metaphyseal irregularity, small irregular epiphyses, flared metaphyses, and platyspondyly with anterior beaking of the vertebral bodies
Windswept lower-limb deformities, genu varum or valgum, and early osteoarthritis are characteristic complications
Cervical spine instability due to odontoid hypoplasia and ligamentous laxity is an important consideration before anaesthesia and physical activity
Diagnosis rests on the radiographic pattern and COMP molecular testing, as the overlap with multiple epiphyseal dysplasia is recognised
reference.pathophysiology: Pseudoachondroplasia is caused by dominant variants in COMP, a glycoprotein of the cartilage extracellular matrix. Mutant protein is retained within the endoplasmic reticulum of chondrocytes rather than being secreted, forming characteristic inclusions and provoking cellular stress that impairs chondrocyte function and premature cell death. Disrupted cartilage matrix in the growth plates and articular surfaces causes disproportionate short stature, epiphyseal and metaphyseal abnormalities, joint laxity, and premature degenerative joint disease.
additionalInvestigations: Skeletal survey documenting epiphyseal and metaphyseal changes and vertebral beaking
COMP molecular genetic testing to confirm the diagnosis
Flexion-extension cervical spine imaging to assess odontoid hypoplasia and atlantoaxial instability
Lower-limb alignment assessment for windswept and angular deformities
Orthopaedic and physiotherapy review for joint pain and mobility
redFlags: Signs of cervical myelopathy from atlantoaxial instability, especially before anaesthesia
Rapidly progressive lower-limb malalignment impairing walking
Severe early-onset joint pain limiting function
Neurological deficit suggesting spinal cord compression
reference.prognosis: Lifespan and intelligence are normal, but adult stature is significantly reduced and premature osteoarthritis, particularly of the hips and knees, frequently necessitates joint replacement in adulthood. Cervical instability requires vigilance to prevent neurological injury.
pitfalls: Expecting features at birth and dismissing the diagnosis in a normal-appearing neonate
Confusing it with achondroplasia despite the normal facial appearance
Overlooking atlantoaxial instability before anaesthesia or sport
Failing to anticipate and manage early degenerative joint disease
